templates.name: Modifier placement: past participial opener (incl. Compared with that of)
Finite vs nonfinite, finite main verb
Pronoun-antecedent agreement: possessive determiner its/their vs contractions
Finite vs nonfinite, finite second or subordinate verb
Plural vs possessive nouns: one- or two-slot spelling grid
Finite vs nonfinite, to-infinitive (purpose or after “the first”)

items.subtype: Modifier placement: preposition + gerund opener (In + -ing), mid-sentence blank; the larva itself is the right subject, the close foil buries it in a possessive
items.passage: The bioluminescent larva of the Brazilian beetle Phrixothrix hirtus, commonly called the railroad worm, glows yellow-green along its sides when disturbed, a display that entomologists interpret as a warning to potential predators. In stalking millipedes at night, however, ______ a deep red light that its prey is probably unable to detect.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: there is a lantern on the larva’s head that gives off
the larva lights the ground ahead of it with
the larva’s head lights the ground ahead of it with
the ground ahead of the larva is lit by
items.explanation: The opening phrase, “In stalking millipedes at night,” describes whatever stalks the millipedes: the larva. Choice B places “the larva” right after the phrase, so the sentence clearly says that the larva is the one stalking millipedes and lighting the ground ahead of it.

A.why_wrong: The word “there” follows the phrase, so the phrase has nothing it can logically describe; the larva appears only inside a possessive later in the clause.

C.why_wrong: The subject is “the larva’s head,” not the larva, so the sentence illogically says that the head itself stalks millipedes at night.

D.recipe: passive that leaves the wrong noun as subject (V)
D.why_wrong: “The ground ahead of the larva” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the ground is what stalks millipedes at night.

items.notes: Subject: railroad worm larvae (Phrixothrix hirtus) and their red head light, thought to be invisible to the millipedes they hunt (science, biology). Real animal, facts kept general (yellow-green side lanterns lit when disturbed, red head light while hunting, millipede prey). Checked against the live glowworm items (words_in_context w2b4_07, New Zealand glowworm snare threads; command_of_evidence w4b3_13, common glow-worm females attracting males): different animals and premise. Band 7 as 37e5c794 (3.16), the only band-7 preposition + gerund item: the key is the obvious noun, and the closest foil is the possessive built on it (C differs from the key only by “’s head”), with E and V beside it. Opener “In + -ing” is not used by any live R3 item (Despite, By, Instead of, In addition to are). Key is not the longest option.

review.options_tested: all four in the full sentence; only the key is grammatical

band7.why: Same recipe as 37e5c794, the only band-7 preposition + gerund item: key the plain agent, foils an expletive (there is a lantern), a possessive built on the key noun (the larva’s head) and a wrong-noun passive (the ground); every foil states something true about the head light, so only the modifier rule separates them.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: past participial opener (Grounded in ...), passage-final blank; the right subject is the team’s conclusion, not the rock or an expletive
items.passage: In 2009, mineralogist Luca Bindi and his colleagues reported the first known natural quasicrystal—a solid whose atoms form an orderly pattern that never repeats—in a rock from Russia’s Koryak Mountains. Grounded in measurements of oxygen isotopes in the grains surrounding the crystal, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: the rock, the team concluded in 2012, was a fragment of a meteorite.
the rock was identified by the team in 2012 as a fragment of a meteorite.
it was the team’s conclusion in 2012 that the rock was a fragment of a meteorite.
the team’s conclusion in 2012 was that the rock was a fragment of a meteorite.
items.explanation: The opening phrase, “Grounded in measurements of oxygen isotopes in the grains surrounding the crystal,” describes something that can rest on measurements: a conclusion. Choice D places “the team’s conclusion” right after the phrase, so the sentence clearly says that the conclusion, not the rock, was grounded in the measurements.

A.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the rock, with an interrupter
A.why_wrong: “The rock” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the rock itself was grounded in measurements of oxygen isotopes.

B.recipe: passive that leaves the wrong noun as subject (V): the rock
B.why_wrong: “The rock” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the rock itself, rather than the team’s conclusion about it, was grounded in measurements of oxygen isotopes; the team appears only in a “by” phrase.

C.why_wrong: The word “it” follows the phrase, so the phrase has no noun it can logically describe; the conclusion appears only later, inside the clause.

items.notes: Subject: Luca Bindi’s natural quasicrystal (icosahedrite) from the Khatyrka River area of the Koryak Mountains, reported in 2009, shown in 2012 by oxygen isotopes to come from a meteorite (science, mineralogy). Real case, facts kept general (2009 report, Koryak Mountains rock, oxygen isotopes, meteorite origin concluded in 2012). Band 7 as 8b017d4e (3.27) and fced396a (3.26): the right subject is a finding noun phrase (“the team’s conclusion”), and every foil starts with the concrete noun the opener seems to describe (the rock, twice) or an expletive. Opener “Grounded in” is not used by any live R3 item; “Confirmed by” was rejected because a rock can itself be “confirmed” as a meteorite fragment, which would make A defensible, and “Based on” because “Based on ..., the team concluded” is widely accepted usage. Options 12 to 16 words; the key is not the longest. Reviewer: B was “the team concluded in 2012 that ...”; replaced by a passive on “the rock,” because “Grounded in ..., the team concluded” can be defended as loosely as “Based on ...” (people are said to be grounded in evidence), and because the old set (interrupter, agent “concluded,” “it was,” nominal key) copied live w3b3_02 (chickadees, “Drawn from recordings”). The set now follows 8b017d4e: no agent foil, two wrong-noun foils on the rock, an expletive, a finding noun phrase as key. “Drawn from” and “Derived from” are both used by live R3 items (w3b3_02, w1b3_02), so “Grounded in” stays. Checked against live w2b1_02 (Winchcombe meteorite, orbit from doorbell cameras): different premise.

fixes: replaced B “the team concluded in 2012 that ...” (agent foil defensible like a “Based on” opener, and the old option set copied live w3b3_02) with “the rock was identified by the team in 2012 as ...”; B why_wrong, subtype, explanation and notes updated
review.options_tested: all four in the full sentence; only the key is grammatical

band7.why: After the fix, the recipe of 8b017d4e (Supported by analyses ...): a support opener whose right subject is a finding noun phrase (the team’s conclusion), two natural foils on the concrete noun (the rock, with an interrupter and in the passive) and an expletive that also contains “the team’s conclusion”; no agent foil, so no “Based on” defence.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: missing main verb after a long subject holding a relative clause and a whose clause with their own verbs
items.passage: Gelatinous colonies of bacteria known as snottites dangle from the ceilings of Cueva de Villa Luz, a sulfur-rich cave in southern Mexico. The sulfuric acid that drips from the colonies, whose microbes metabolize hydrogen sulfide gas emerging from underground springs, ______ the surrounding limestone, gradually enlarging the cave’s passages.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the second sentence is “The sulfuric acid,” and everything up to the blank describes that acid, including a “that” clause and a “whose” clause. The sentence still needs a main verb for “The sulfuric acid.” Choice C supplies the finite present tense verb “eats away at,” so the sentence says what the acid does to the limestone.

A.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed: -ing
A.why_wrong: The participle “eating away at” cannot serve as the main verb of the sentence, so the sentence would be a fragment with no main verb for “The sulfuric acid.”

B.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed: to + base
B.why_wrong: The infinitive “to eat away at” cannot serve as the main verb, so the sentence would have no main verb for “The sulfuric acid.”

D.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed: having + past participle
D.why_wrong: The phrase “having eaten away at” is nonfinite and cannot serve as the main verb, so the sentence would be a fragment.

items.notes: Subject: snottites, acid-dripping bacterial colonies in the sulfur cave Cueva de Villa Luz, Tabasco, Mexico (science, microbiology and geology). Real cave and microbes, facts kept general (colonies feed on hydrogen sulfide from springs, their acid attacks the limestone and enlarges the cave). Band 6 as a75d5984 (3.13), the template’s only band-6 item (no band-7 item exists): canonical set {finite, -ing, to + base, having + participle}; the head “The sulfuric acid” is held open for 19 words by a “that” clause and a “whose” clause whose own finite verbs (drips, metabolize) and the participle “emerging” can make the clause feel complete. Key is the shortest option.

review.options_tested: all four in the full sentence; only the key is grammatical

band7.why: R2_finite_main has no band-7 official item (band7 appendix), so it cannot be band 7; a strong band 6 as a75d5984, with the head 19 words before the blank behind a that clause and a whose clause with their own finite verbs.

items.subtype: Pronoun-antecedent: possessive determiner its vs their and contractions; antecedent 15 words before the blank with plural nouns between
items.passage: Tenants of the Fuggerei in Augsburg, Germany, still pay an annual rent equivalent to one Rhenish guilder, approximately 0.88 euros. Every night at ten o’clock, the Fuggerei, a walled settlement of rowhouses that the merchant Jakob Fugger established in 1516, locks ______ gates; anyone returning later must pay the watchman a small fee.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The blank refers back to “the Fuggerei,” the subject of the clause, which is singular: the gates belong to the settlement. Choice A supplies the singular possessive determiner “its,” so the sentence says that the settlement locks its own gates.

B.why_wrong: “It’s” is a contraction of “it is” or “it has,” so “locks it’s gates” makes no sense; the blank needs a possessive.

C.recipe: wrong number pronoun: their (attracted by rowhouses)
C.why_wrong: “Their” is plural, but the gates belong to “the Fuggerei,” a single settlement; the plural nouns before the blank (“Tenants,” “euros,” “rowhouses”) are not what owns the gates.

D.why_wrong: “They’re” is a contraction of “they are” and is plural, so it can neither show possession nor refer to the singular “Fuggerei.”

items.notes: Subject: the Fuggerei in Augsburg, social housing founded by Jakob Fugger in 1516, annual rent of one Rhenish guilder (0.88 euros), gates locked at ten at night (social science and history). Real place, facts kept general. Band 6 as 3bceeb93 (3.4): antecedent is the clause subject, here 16 words before the blank behind an appositive holding the plural “rowhouses” and a relative clause; plural “Tenants” opens the passage; options the 2 x 2 grid. The tail uses singular “anyone” so “their” has no plural antecedent after the blank. Not the 3.22 skeleton (no “Like ______ peer”). Key is the shortest option.

review.options_tested: all four in the full sentence; only the key is grammatical

band7.why: Plan band 6. As 3bceeb93 but harder: the antecedent is the clause subject 16 words back behind an appositive holding “rowhouses,” with plural “Tenants” opening the passage; the 2 x 2 grid.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: second verb of a compound predicate, split from the first by a participial phrase (using winches ...)
items.passage: Engineer Vladimir Shukhov’s hyperboloid broadcasting tower in Moscow, completed in 1922, was constructed without cranes. Workers assembled each of its five upper sections at ground level inside the structure’s base and then, using winches mounted atop the previously erected sections, ______ it upward into position.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject “Workers” has two actions joined by “and then”: they “assembled” each section and then lifted it. The second verb must be finite and match the first, the past tense “assembled.” Choice D supplies the past tense verb “hoisted,” completing the compound predicate; the phrase “using winches mounted atop the previously erected sections” only describes how they did it.

A.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed: -ing
A.why_wrong: The participle “hoisting” cannot serve as the second main verb after “and then,” so the compound predicate would be incomplete; it also echoes “using,” which tempts a parallel -ing form.

B.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed: to + base
B.why_wrong: The infinitive “to hoist” cannot pair with “assembled” after “and then,” so the sentence would lack its second main verb.

C.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed: having + past participle
C.why_wrong: “Having hoisted” is nonfinite and cannot serve as the second verb joined to “assembled” by “and then.”

items.notes: Subject: the Shukhov (Shabolovka) radio tower, Moscow, completed 1922, raised without cranes by assembling upper sections inside the base and winching them up (history of engineering). Real structure, facts kept general. Band 6 as b74f676f (2.1, band 6): canonical set {finite past, -ing, to + base, having + participle}; the participial phrase “using winches ... sections” (7 words) sits between “and then” and the blank, so the -ing foil reads as parallel to “using.” The key is the -ed form, so no -ed foil can be read as a reduced relative. Key is the shortest option.

review.options_tested: all four in the full sentence; only the key is grammatical

band7.why: R2_finite_second has no band-7 official item, so it cannot be band 7; a strong band 6 as b74f676f, with a 7-word -ing phrase (using winches ...) between “and then” and the blank that makes the -ing foil look parallel.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: -ing participial phrase of result after a complete clause and a comma
items.passage: Beginning in the 1950s, American sculptor Louise Nevelson collected discarded wood—chair legs, banisters, crate slats, and moldings—from the streets of New York City. She arranged the fragments in stacked compartments and painted each assemblage a uniform matte black, ______ viewers to focus on shapes and shadows rather than on the objects’ original functions.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The words before the comma already form a complete sentence: “She arranged the fragments in stacked compartments and painted each assemblage a uniform matte black.” What follows must be a phrase, not a new clause. Choice B supplies the participle “encouraging,” which begins a phrase describing the effect of painting everything black.

A.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed: past
A.why_wrong: “Encouraged” is a finite past tense verb with no subject or conjunction of its own; after the comma it would leave a third verb tacked onto the compound predicate without “and.”

C.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed: had + past participle
C.why_wrong: “Had encouraged” is a finite verb, so the sentence would join another verb to the complete clause with only a comma; the past perfect also wrongly places the effect before the painting.

D.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed: present -s
D.why_wrong: “Encourages” is a finite present tense verb with no subject of its own; after the comma and the complete clause, it cannot begin the phrase the sentence needs.

items.notes: Subject: Louise Nevelson’s black wall assemblages of scavenged New York wood (arts, sculpture). Real artist, facts kept general (wood scraps from city streets from the 1950s, stacked boxes painted a single black). Band 6 as a30567fd (2.9, band 6): complete clause, comma, -ing result phrase; options {-ing, past, had + participle, present -s} after the model’s {earned, had earned, earning, earn}. The clause before the comma is long (two coordinated verbs), so a finite foil can feel like a third verb in the series. 18 words follow the blank. The template’s band-7 setting (absolute phrase, 81f09e07) was not planned for this cell. Not the model’s “earning her the moniker” wording.

review.options_tested: all four in the full sentence; only the key is grammatical

band7.why: Plan band 6. As a30567fd: complete clause with two coordinated verbs, comma, -ing result phrase, 18 words after the blank; not the absolute-phrase setting of the band-7 items 81f09e07 and c88ba1b7.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular head “correspondence” followed by a prepositional phrase holding the plural “pioneers”
items.passage: Writer May Ziadeh, who lived in Cairo, and poet Kahlil Gibran, who lived in New York, exchanged letters from 1912 until Gibran’s death in 1931 but never met in person. The correspondence between these two pioneers of modern Arabic literature ______ a relationship conducted entirely on paper.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the second sentence is the singular noun “correspondence”; the phrase “between these two pioneers of modern Arabic literature” only describes it. A singular subject needs a singular verb, so choice A, “reveals,” is correct.

B.why_wrong: “Reveal” is a plural verb, but the subject is the singular “correspondence,” not the plural “pioneers” in the phrase that follows it.

C.why_wrong: “Are revealing” is plural, so it does not agree with the singular subject “correspondence.”

D.why_wrong: “Have revealed” is plural, so it does not agree with the singular subject “correspondence.”

items.notes: Subject: the letters between May Ziadeh (Cairo) and Kahlil Gibran (New York), 1912 to 1931, who never met (literature). Real writers, facts kept general. Medium as 2.7 and 2.11: singular head followed by an “of”/“between” phrase with a plural noun (“pioneers”) as the attractor; options one verb in four forms {V-s, V, are V-ing, have V-ed}. First sentence is a compound subject with two “who” clauses, so a plural verb sounds natural just before. Key is not the longest option.

review.options_tested: all four in the full sentence; only the key is grammatical

items.subtype: Pronoun-antecedent: singular object pronoun “it” for “the microbe,” with the plural nouns “amoebas,” “viruses” and “researchers” nearby
items.passage: In 1992, researchers found a microbe living inside amoebas from a cooling tower in Bradford, England. Because the microbe, unlike most viruses, was large enough to be seen with a light microscope, researchers classified ______ as a bacterium; only in 2003 did scientists identify the microbe as a giant virus, now called mimivirus.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The pronoun in the blank refers to “the microbe,” the single organism that the researchers mistook for a bacterium. A singular noun needs a singular pronoun, so choice C, “it,” is correct: researchers classified the microbe as a bacterium.

A.recipe: wrong number pronoun: them (attracted by viruses, amoebas)
A.why_wrong: “Them” is plural, but the thing classified is the singular “microbe,” as “as a bacterium” also shows; the plural nouns nearby (“viruses,” “amoebas”) are not what was classified.

B.why_wrong: “Those” is plural and points to some other group, so it cannot refer back to the single microbe.

D.why_wrong: “These” is plural, so it cannot refer back to the single microbe that researchers classified “as a bacterium.”

items.notes: Subject: mimivirus, found in 1992 in amoebas from a Bradford cooling tower, first classified as a bacterium, identified as a giant virus in 2003 (science, microbiology). Real case, facts kept general (the French team is not named). The boundaries w5b5_04 writer withdrew the same subject in favour of this claim. Medium as 2.15 and 2.3: the antecedent sits in the same sentence and a plural noun (“most viruses”) lies between it and the blank; options {it, them, those, these}, number plus kind as in 2.15 without copying its set. Key is the shortest option.

review.options_tested: all four in the full sentence; only the key is grammatical

items.subtype: Plural vs possessive: two-slot grid, singular possessor named earlier (the painter) + plain plural noun
items.passage: American painter Kay Sage, who joined the Surrealist circle in Paris in the late 1930s and later settled in Connecticut, seldom depicted human figures. Instead, the ______ show desolate plains crowded with scaffolding, folds of draped fabric, and towers that appear to be perpetually under construction.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The blank names the canvases that belong to one painter, Kay Sage. The singular possessive “painter’s” shows that the canvases are hers, and “canvases” is a plain plural that owns nothing. Choice D is the only option that spells both words this way.

A.why_wrong: “Painters” has no apostrophe, so it is a plain plural and does not show that the canvases belong to Sage.

B.recipe: needless apostrophe on a plain plural
B.why_wrong: “Painter’s” is correct, but “canvas’s” is a singular possessive, and the canvases do not own anything in the sentence.

C.recipe: wrong possessor number and needless apostrophe
C.why_wrong: “Painters’” is a plural possessive, but only one painter is discussed, and “canvases’” adds a possessive to a noun that owns nothing.

items.notes: Subject: Kay Sage’s figureless Surrealist landscapes of scaffolding, drapery and unfinished towers (arts, painting). Real artist, facts kept general (Paris Surrealists in the late 1930s, later life in Connecticut). Medium as 2.24 (“author’s political writings”): one named person earlier makes the possessor singular, and the grid offers a missing apostrophe, a needless one, and a plural possessor with an extra apostrophe. Key is not the longest option.

review.options_tested: all four in the full sentence; only the key is grammatical

items.subtype: Tense: simple past for a dated event (in August 1934) inside a present-tense main clause (Historians still regard ...)
items.passage: In the early 1930s, naturalist William Beebe and engineer Otis Barton investigated the waters off Bermuda from inside the bathysphere, a steel sphere suspended from a ship by a cable. Historians still regard the descent that the two men ______ in August 1934, to a depth of 923 meters, as a milestone in oceanographic exploration.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The descent took place at a specific time in the past, “in August 1934.” An action completed at a stated past time takes the simple past, so choice B, “made,” is correct, even though the main verb “regard” is in the present tense because historians hold that view today.

A.recipe: present perfect where a dated past is needed
A.why_wrong: The present perfect “have made” is not used with a specific past time such as “in August 1934.”

C.why_wrong: “Will make” places the descent in the future, but it happened in 1934.

D.why_wrong: “Are making” describes something happening now, not a descent completed in 1934.

items.notes: Subject: William Beebe and Otis Barton’s bathysphere dives off Bermuda, record descent to 923 meters in August 1934 (history of science). Real people and event, facts kept general. Medium as 2.12 (“historians have praised it, noting that Lincoln ______”): a present-tense frame about later judgment tempts a present or present perfect form, and the dated cue sits right after the blank. Key is the shortest option.

review.options_tested: all four in the full sentence; only the key is grammatical

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular head followed by an appositive holding the plurals “buildings” and “residents” and a relative clause
items.passage: Kowloon Walled City, a cluster of roughly 300 interconnected buildings in Hong Kong that housed some 33,000 residents on just 2.6 hectares, ______ demolished in 1993 and 1994. A public park, which preserves architectural remnants of the old settlement such as its south gate, now occupies the site.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the first sentence is “Kowloon Walled City,” a single place; the long phrase after it (“a cluster of ... 2.6 hectares”) only renames and describes it. A singular subject needs a singular verb, and the dates call for the past tense, so choice C, “was,” is correct.

A.why_wrong: “Were” is plural, so it agrees with the nearby plurals “buildings” and “residents” rather than with the singular subject “Kowloon Walled City.”

B.why_wrong: “Have been” is plural, so it does not agree with the singular subject “Kowloon Walled City.”

D.why_wrong: “Are” is plural, so it does not agree with the singular subject “Kowloon Walled City.”

items.notes: Subject: Kowloon Walled City, Hong Kong, about 33,000 residents on 2.6 hectares, demolished 1993 to 1994, now a park keeping remnants such as the south gate (history and urban studies). Real place, facts kept general. Checked against live FSS w3b1_11 (Shibam, a walled city of mud-brick towers): different place and premise. Medium as 2.21 and 2.16: singular head plus an appositive full of plural nouns and a relative clause with its own verb (“housed”); be-family options {was, were, are, have been}. Key ties for shortest.

review.options_tested: all four in the full sentence; only the key is grammatical

items.subtype: Pronoun-antecedent: possessive determiner its vs their and contractions; singular subject behind a participial phrase holding the plural “states”
items.passage: The Trans-Australian Railway, completed in 1917 to connect the eastern states with Western Australia, crosses the treeless Nullarbor Plain on ______ way west. Across that plain, the track stretches without a single bend for 478 kilometers, forming the longest straight section of railway track in the world.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The blank refers to “the Trans-Australian Railway,” the subject of the sentence, which is a single rail line. The way west is the railway’s own, so the sentence needs the singular possessive determiner “its.” Choice A is correct.

B.recipe: wrong number pronoun: their (attracted by states)
B.why_wrong: “Their” is plural, but the way west belongs to “the Trans-Australian Railway,” one rail line, not to the plural “states” in the phrase that says why it was built.

C.why_wrong: “They’re” means “they are,” so it cannot show possession, and it is plural.

D.why_wrong: “It’s” means “it is” or “it has,” so “on it’s way west” makes no sense; the blank needs the possessive “its.”

items.notes: Subject: the Trans-Australian Railway (completed 1917) and its 478-kilometer straight across the Nullarbor Plain, the longest straight stretch of railway in the world (social science, history of transport). Real line, facts kept general. Reviewer replacement for Burushaski noun classes, a concept twin of live FSS w4b1_10 (Zulu “organizes its nouns into grammatical classes”). Grepped Nullarbor, Trans-Australian, longest straight: no live item; the live railway items (Japanese station melodies, African port lines, rack railways, plague along Manchurian railways) have other premises. Medium: antecedent is the clause subject, with the plural “states” as the attractor; options the 2 x 2 grid as 0bcb4417 (2.6). Not 2.6’s pronoun-before-antecedent frame. Key is the shortest option.

fixes: new subject: Burushaski noun classes was a concept twin of live FSS w4b1_10 (Zulu nouns in grammatical classes); rewritten on the Trans-Australian Railway and the Nullarbor straight, same template, key A and option order; subtype, explanation, distractors, notes and word_count rewritten; claim appended and Burushaski withdrawn in claims.txt
review.options_tested: all four in the full sentence; only the key is grammatical

items.subtype: Tense: simple present for a recurring event (Approximately every eighteen months) in a present-tense description
items.passage: Loki Patera, a volcanic depression roughly 200 kilometers across on Jupiter’s moon Io, is thought to contain an enormous lake of molten lava. Approximately every eighteen months, the lake ______ dramatically in infrared observations as fresh lava spreads across its cooled surface.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The passage describes something that happens again and again: “Approximately every eighteen months,” the lake changes, and the rest of the sentence is in the present tense (“spreads”). A repeated, ongoing event takes the simple present, so choice D, “brightens,” is correct.

A.recipe: simple past where present is needed
A.why_wrong: “Brightened” places the event in the past, but the passage describes a cycle that continues, in the present tense (“is thought,” “spreads”).

B.recipe: past perfect where the cue is present
B.why_wrong: “Had brightened” describes an action completed before another past event, but nothing in the passage is set in the past.

C.why_wrong: “Will have brightened” describes an action completed before a future time, which does not fit a regular cycle described in the present.

items.notes: Subject: Loki Patera on Io, a lava lake about 200 km across that brightens roughly every 540 days (science, planetary geology). Real feature, facts kept general (eighteen months for the roughly 540-day cycle). Grepped Io volcanism: no live item (the only Io hit is a moon-classification table, command_of_evidence w3b3_22). Easy as 1.17 (“Each year ... they ______”) and 1.37: an explicit recurrence cue plus a present-tense frame; distractor set after 1.1 (past perfect, future perfect). Key is not the longest option.

review.options_tested: all four in the full sentence; only the key is grammatical

items.subtype: Tense: simple present for a permanent state (a mountain rises ...) in a present-tense description
items.passage: The giant asteroid Vesta’s southern hemisphere is dominated by Rheasilvia, an impact basin roughly 500 kilometers wide. At the center of the basin, a mountain formed by the impact ______ about 22 kilometers above the surrounding floor, more than twice the height of Mount Everest.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The passage describes Vesta as it is now, in the present tense (“is dominated”). The mountain still stands at the center of the basin, so its height is a present fact, and choice A, the simple present “rises,” is correct.

B.recipe: past perfect where the cue is present
B.why_wrong: “Had risen” describes something completed before another past event, but the passage describes the basin as it is today.

C.why_wrong: “Will rise” suggests the mountain does not yet reach that height, but the passage describes it as already standing.

D.why_wrong: “Was rising” describes an action in progress at some past moment, not a permanent feature of the present landscape.

items.notes: Subject: Rheasilvia, the giant impact basin on Vesta, and its central peak about 22 km high (science, planetary geology). Real feature, facts kept general. Checked against live command_of_evidence w2b2_21 (Vesta and Pallas discovery dates in a table): different premise. Easy as 1.25 and 1.37: a general present description with a present-tense frame; the simple past is left out of the set so no option is defensible. Key is the shortest option.

review.options_tested: all four in the full sentence; only the key is grammatical

items.subtype: Pronoun-antecedent: singular subject pronoun “it” for “the novel,” antecedent earlier in the same sentence
items.passage: Polish writer Bolesław Prus’s The Doll was originally serialized in a Warsaw newspaper between 1887 and 1889. Because the novel provides a remarkably detailed portrait of the city’s nineteenth-century society, ______ is still consulted by historians as well as enjoyed by readers of fiction.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The pronoun in the blank refers to “the novel,” The Doll, a single book. A singular noun needs a singular pronoun, so choice C, “it,” is correct: the novel is still consulted by historians and enjoyed by readers.

A.why_wrong: “They” is plural, but the thing still read today is the single novel, The Doll.

B.why_wrong: “Those” is plural and points to some other group, so it cannot refer to the single novel.

D.why_wrong: “Both” refers to two things, but the sentence describes a single novel, The Doll.

items.notes: Subject: Bolesław Prus’s novel The Doll (Lalka), serialized in a Warsaw newspaper (Kurier Codzienny) from 1887 to 1889, valued for its portrait of Warsaw society (literature). Real novel, facts kept general. Easy as 1.39 (“______ involves”) and 1.26: the antecedent is named just before in the same sentence with no rival noun, and the verb after the blank is fixed; options {it, they, those, both}, as 1.39 and 1.33 mix personal and demonstrative pronouns. Key is the shortest option.

review.options_tested: all four in the full sentence; only the key is grammatical

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular name followed by a short singular appositive
items.passage: Bislama, an official language of the Pacific nation of Vanuatu, ______ named after bêche-de-mer, a French term for the sea cucumbers that nineteenth-century traders harvested on coral reefs throughout the region. Many early speakers acquired the language while laboring on plantations in Australia and Fiji.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the first sentence is “Bislama,” the name of a single language; the phrase “an official language of the Pacific nation of Vanuatu” only describes it. A singular subject needs a singular verb, so choice B, “was,” is correct.

A.why_wrong: “Are” is plural, so it does not agree with the singular subject “Bislama.”

C.why_wrong: “Were” is plural, so it does not agree with the singular subject “Bislama.”

D.why_wrong: “Have been” is plural, so it does not agree with the singular subject “Bislama.”

items.notes: Subject: Bislama, an official language of Vanuatu, named after bêche-de-mer (the sea cucumber trade), spread through plantation labour in Queensland and Fiji (social science, linguistics). Real language, facts kept general. The premise is the name’s origin, not creole status or language diversity, so it does not echo the live creole items (Kristang, Palenquero, Chavacano) or the Tok Pisin note in rhetorical_synthesis w3b5_21. Easy as 1.4 (name + short appositive, no number clash); be-family options. Key is the shortest option.

review.options_tested: all four in the full sentence; only the key is grammatical

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: plural head right before the blank, after a participial opener
items.passage: In the late 1920s, Polish sculptor Katarzyna Kobro produced a series of abstract works she titled Spatial Compositions. Constructed from bent and painted sheets of steel, the sculptures ______ intended to open outward into the surrounding environment rather than enclose a solid, self-contained mass.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the second sentence is the plural noun “sculptures,” which comes right before the blank. A plural subject needs a plural verb, and the sentence describes works made in the 1920s, so choice D, “were,” is correct.

A.why_wrong: “Was” is singular, so it does not agree with the plural subject “sculptures.”

B.why_wrong: “Is” is singular, so it does not agree with the plural subject “sculptures.”

C.why_wrong: “Has been” is singular, so it does not agree with the plural subject “sculptures.”

items.notes: Subject: Katarzyna Kobro’s Spatial Compositions, painted steel sculptures of the late 1920s that open into the surrounding space (arts, sculpture). Real artist, facts kept general. Easy as 1.28 and 1.7 (plural head, key “were”); the opener “Constructed from ... steel” has a singular noun but sits before the subject, not between it and the verb. Key is not the longest option.

review.options_tested: all four in the full sentence; only the key is grammatical

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular title followed by a singular appositive (a play by ...)
items.passage: The People of the Cave (1933), a play by Egyptian writer Tawfiq al-Hakim, ______ an ancient legend about Christians who take refuge in a cave to escape persecution and awaken some three centuries later. In al-Hakim’s interpretation, the sleepers are unable to adjust to the transformed society they encounter.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the first sentence is The People of the Cave, the title of a single play, as the appositive “a play by Egyptian writer Tawfiq al-Hakim” confirms. A singular subject needs a singular verb, so choice C, “adapts,” is correct.

A.why_wrong: “Adapt” is a plural verb, but the subject is a single play; the title’s plural-sounding words (“People”) do not make it plural.

B.why_wrong: “Are adapting” is plural, so it does not agree with the singular subject, the play.

D.why_wrong: “Have adapted” is plural, so it does not agree with the singular subject, the play.

items.notes: Subject: Tawfiq al-Hakim’s 1933 play The People of the Cave (Ahl al-Kahf), based on the legend of the sleepers in the cave (literature, drama). Real play, facts kept general. Easy as 1.20 (singular name + appositive, key V-s); a title with a plural-looking noun (“People”) is the only trap. Lexical options {V-s, V, are V-ing, have V-ed}. Key is not the longest option.

review.options_tested: all four in the full sentence; only the key is grammatical

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: missing main verb after a short plural subject
items.passage: Silver coins minted in Spain’s American colonies, especially Mexico, circulated widely in the early United States. These Spanish dollars ______ legal tender in the country until 1857, when Congress passed legislation ending the legal status of foreign currency.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The second sentence has a subject, “These Spanish dollars,” but no main verb unless the blank supplies one. Choice A supplies the finite past tense verb “remained,” which tells what the coins did until 1857.

B.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed: -ing
B.why_wrong: “Remaining” is a participle and cannot serve as the main verb, so the sentence would be a fragment.

C.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed: to + base
C.why_wrong: “To remain” is an infinitive and cannot serve as the main verb, so the sentence would have no main verb.

D.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed: having + past participle
D.why_wrong: “Having remained” is nonfinite and cannot serve as the main verb, so the sentence would be a fragment.

items.notes: Subject: Spanish silver dollars, minted mostly in Mexico, legal tender in the United States until the Coinage Act of 1857 (social science, economic history). Real history, facts kept general. Replaces the withdrawn Lukyanov water integrator claim (a hydraulic-computer twin of MONIAC, boundaries w5b4_23). Easy as 1.31 and 1.23: short subject, blank in the main-verb slot; canonical set {finite, -ing, to + base, having + participle}. Key is not the longest option.

review.options_tested: all four in the full sentence; only the key is grammatical

items.subtype: Plural vs possessive: two-slot grid, singular possessor (one merchant’s) + singular noun
items.passage: Founded in 1609, the Bank of Amsterdam allowed merchants to settle their debts without physically exchanging coins, which at the time varied considerably in weight and purity. Whenever a merchant made a payment, the bank’s clerks simply transferred the amount from one ______ to another’s in the institution’s ledgers.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The words “from one” and “to another’s” show that a single merchant owns a single account. The singular possessive “merchant’s” shows the ownership, and “account” needs no apostrophe because it owns nothing. Choice B is the only option that spells both words this way.

A.why_wrong: “Merchants” has no apostrophe, so it does not show that the account belongs to the merchant, and it is plural after “one.”

C.recipe: needless apostrophe on the possessed noun
C.why_wrong: “Merchant’s” is correct, but “account’s” is possessive, and the account does not own anything in the sentence.

D.recipe: wrong possessor number and plural noun
D.why_wrong: “Merchants’ accounts” refers to several merchants and several accounts, but “one” calls for a single merchant’s single account.

items.notes: Subject: the Bank of Amsterdam (Wisselbank), founded 1609, settling merchants’ payments by ledger transfer instead of coins of uneven weight and purity (history and economics). Real institution, facts kept general. Easy as 1.10 (number cue right before the blank, “one ... another’s”) with the two-slot grid of 1.16. Key is not the longest option.

review.options_tested: all four in the full sentence; only the key is grammatical

items.subtype: Plural vs possessive: two-slot grid, singular possessor (the town) + plain plural noun
items.passage: Radburn, New Jersey, planned in 1929 as a “town for the motor age,” separated pedestrian paths from automobile traffic so that children could walk to school without crossing a major road. Many of the ______ were oriented with their living rooms facing shared parkland and their kitchens facing dead-end streets.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The blank names the houses that belong to one town, Radburn. The singular possessive “town’s” shows that the houses are the town’s, and “houses” is a plain plural that owns nothing. Choice C is the only option that spells both words this way.

A.why_wrong: “Towns” has no apostrophe, so it is a plain plural and does not show that the houses belong to Radburn.

B.recipe: needless apostrophe on a plain plural
B.why_wrong: “Town’s” is correct, but “house’s” is a singular possessive, and the houses do not own anything here; “Many of the” also calls for a plural.

D.recipe: wrong possessor number and needless apostrophe
D.why_wrong: “Towns’” is a plural possessive, but only one town is discussed, and “houses’” adds a possessive to a noun that owns nothing.

items.notes: Subject: Radburn, New Jersey, the 1929 “town for the motor age” planned by Clarence Stein and Henry Wright with houses turned toward shared parkland and footpaths separated from roads (social science, urban planning). Real town, facts kept general. Checked against live boundaries w1b3_10 (Barcelona superblocks): different place and premise. Easy as 1.16 (“photographer’s early photos”): full two-slot grid with a singular possessor. Key is not the longest option.

review.options_tested: all four in the full sentence; only the key is grammatical

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: to-infinitive of purpose after a complete clause
items.passage: In 1961, geologists participating in Project Mohole operated a floating drilling platform off Mexico’s Guadalupe Island, where the Pacific Ocean is more than 3,500 meters deep. They penetrated approximately 180 meters into the seafloor ______ samples of the basalt beneath its sediments.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The words before the blank already form a complete clause: “They penetrated approximately 180 meters into the seafloor.” The blank must begin a phrase that gives the purpose of the drilling, not a second main verb. Choice D, the infinitive “to collect,” does this.

A.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed: past
A.why_wrong: “Collected” is a finite verb, so the sentence would have two main verbs, “penetrated” and “collected,” with nothing joining them.

B.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed: present
B.why_wrong: “Collect” is a finite present tense verb, so the sentence would have two main verbs, “penetrated” and “collect,” with nothing joining them.

C.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed: are + -ing
C.why_wrong: “Are collecting” is a finite verb phrase, so the sentence would again have two main verbs without a conjunction.

items.notes: Subject: Project Mohole’s 1961 test drilling from the CUSS I off Guadalupe Island, Mexico, in about 3,500 m of water, about 180 m into the seafloor to reach basalt (science, geology). Real project, facts kept general. Easy as 1.22 and 1.27: purpose infinitive after a complete clause; options {to + base, V-ed, V, are V-ing}, every finite form agreeing with “They” as 1.22’s set agrees with its subject. Key is not the longest option.

review.options_tested: all four in the full sentence; only the key is grammatical

items.subtype: Tense: past perfect for an action earlier than a past verb (some visitors suspected)
items.passage: In 1880, painter Arkhip Kuindzhi exhibited a single landscape, Moonlit Night on the Dnieper, in a darkened hall in Saint Petersburg, illuminating it with a concentrated beam of electric light. The moonlight on the river appeared so luminous that some visitors suspected Kuindzhi ______ a lamp behind the canvas.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The visitors’ suspicion is in the past (“suspected”), and what they suspected would have happened before that moment: the lamp would already have been hidden when they saw the painting. An action completed before another past action takes the past perfect, so choice A, “had hidden,” is correct.

B.recipe: present simple where the past perfect is needed
B.why_wrong: “Hides” is the present tense, but the passage describes visitors’ thoughts in 1880, so the earlier action needs the past perfect.

C.why_wrong: “Will have been hiding” points to the future, but the event took place in 1880.

D.why_wrong: “Is hiding” describes something happening now, not an action completed before the visitors’ suspicion in 1880.

items.notes: Subject: Arkhip Kuindzhi’s 1880 one-painting show of Moonlit Night on the Dnieper in a darkened Saint Petersburg hall, lit by electric light, with visitors looking for a hidden lamp (arts, painting). Real event, facts kept general; no nationality given for the painter (Mariupol-born, often called Russian or Ukrainian). Easy as 1.24 (“which ... Planté ______ fifteen years earlier”): a past verb in the same sentence sets the earlier past; the long distractor “will have been hiding” follows 1.1. Key is not the longest option.

review.options_tested: all four in the full sentence; only the key is grammatical

items.subtype: Tense: simple past for a dated event (In 1886)
items.passage: Until the 1880s, newspaper compositors assembled type by hand, one individual letter at a time. In 1886, the New York Tribune ______ the first newspaper to adopt the Linotype, a typesetting machine invented by Ottmar Mergenthaler that cast complete lines of type from molten metal.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence describes an event at a specific time in the past, “In 1886.” An event completed at a stated past time takes the simple past, so choice B, “became,” is correct.

A.recipe: present simple where a dated past is needed
A.why_wrong: “Becomes” is the present tense, but the event happened in 1886.

C.why_wrong: “Will become” places the event in the future, but it happened in 1886.

D.recipe: present perfect where a dated past is needed
D.why_wrong: The present perfect “has become” is not used with a specific past time such as “In 1886.”

items.notes: Subject: the New York Tribune’s 1886 adoption of Ottmar Mergenthaler’s Linotype, which cast whole lines of type (history of technology). Real event, facts kept general. Easy as 1.13 and 1.32: an explicit date in the same sentence; options {past, present, future, present perfect}. Key is the shortest option.

review.options_tested: all four in the full sentence; only the key is grammatical
